session_title: 'Mental Health' and 'Worry' Management in the Context of Global Mobility
theme: 健康-知识分子的身心状态

content.text: (Sending an image) Gu Zhizhou, I’ve been reflecting on my information consumption habits lately. Look, this is my screen time report from the past seven days. I set a rule for myself to read only two hours of high-quality sources daily, but in reality, I’ve been drowning in a sea of information. This reminds me of our discussion on "algorithmic aesthetics" when selecting the annual keywords (Session 10)—platform recommendations have made me passively absorb too many fragmented pieces. I’ve even started to question whether the public comments I write hold any real meaning, much like how we questioned symbolic relief when discussing critiques of consumer culture (Session 8). Given your long-term experience in handling complex cross-cultural information, how do you avoid this kind of "depth fatigue" and cognitive exhaustion?

I've designated every Sunday as my 'Low Information Input Day,' using this 'Information Diet List' app to manage it. In my cross-border work, I've found that excessive connectivity can actually weaken deep thinking abilities, much like the 'administrative battles' we discussed regarding pet migration (Session 6)—information overload is also a mental administrative burden. 😌

This method is quite good. It reminds me of our previous discussion about traveling in Uzbekistan (Session 8), where you maintained keen observation in that cultural crossroads, perhaps related to this sense of restraint. Just like the photos of architectural fusion you shared at the time, selective attention is needed to capture the deeper beauty.

Yes, just like during that trip when I sent photos of architecture (Session 9), I was actually practicing selective attention. Last week, I tried a "digital detox," and on the third day, I felt very anxious, constantly worried about missing important information. But later, I realized that true detachment isn’t about avoidance, but about connecting selectively. 😌 This reminds me of the experience at the Kyoto ryōtei (Session 4), that kind of "silent communication"—deep understanding requires actively creating a quiet space, not passively receiving all the noise.

Your method reminds me of this. Detachment isn't about completely disconnecting, but about establishing boundaries. The three questions on this sticky note are what I ask myself before writing, helping to filter out irrelevant information. Just like when we analyze film narratives (Session 2), we need to first identify the core theme before delving deeper into the text.

This reminds me of our discussion on pet migration (Session 6), where those policy comparison charts actually serve as a tool for information filtering—extracting key points from complex processes. You mentioned writing; how exactly do you use it to relax? Is it like when we talked about the politics of food culture (Session 5), where writing helps organize chaotic thoughts?

Besides those methods, I also choose writing to relax myself. For example, this book "Writing for Myself" is not an academic output but a pure record of feelings, much like the silent exchange we had when discussing Kyoto cuisine (Session 4)—not aimed at publication, but for inner organization. It reminds me of what you said when sharing the handwritten recipe photos: "It feels warmer than a digital menu."

I can also try to relax myself through writing. In the context of transnational mobility, sometimes the 'flow' experience of caring for a cat can be more rejuvenating than reading a theoretical book, much like the photo of the orange cat overlooking the city in Session 7—it taught me that simple companionship holds more healing power than complex information. This reminds me of our discussion about emotional anchors (Session 7) and how pets provide an unconditional sense of presence.

Indeed, the theory of emotional anchors (Session 7) applies here as well. Both writing and pet care offer a sense of controllable immersion, countering information overload. Just as we observed in our analysis of Shen Teng's films (Session 3), simple emotional connections often resonate more deeply than complex narratives. Regarding the 'information diet checklist' you shared earlier, what specific principles does it include? Is it as systematic as your comparison of ticketing platforms (Session 1)?

I primarily set up three types of filters: first, time constraints, such as low-information input days; second, source quality, prioritizing in-depth long-form content and cross-cultural comparisons, similar to the film narrative analysis in Session 2—I’ve shared multilingual material comparisons, which I now use to filter information; third, emotional regulation, using emojis to mark reading states, which continues my habit of using emojis to express complex emotions. 📊

Profound and thought-provoking, this reminds me of our debate on 'algorithmic aesthetics' and 'locality' during the selection of the annual keywords (Session 10). In essence, it is a practice of information filtering—how to maintain local consciousness within the global flow of information. Does your approach also apply to public commentary writing? Just as when we deconstruct lifestyle brands (Session 8), we first need to filter out the superficial cultural packaging.

Yes, when writing market analysis or cultural commentary, I start by creating an information gap analysis table, similar to the chart on dietary identity narratives in Session 5—breaking down complex phenomena into manageable modules. This helps avoid cognitive exhaustion and maintains a global perspective. 😊 Just like we discussed the pet documentation process (Session 6), systematic handling can reduce anxiety.

From an academically rigorous perspective, I believe the essence of this management is to resist the erosion of "cultural packaging" (Session 11). When information is commodified, much like how refined cuisine is reconstructed as a tourism product (Session 5), the mental well-being of individuals requires the active construction of boundaries. This reminds me of the Kyoto garden photos you shared (Session 4)—the white sand and black stones of the dry landscape are a form of minimalist boundary art.

Completely agree! Just like the landscape paintings and porcelain discussed in Session 9, the deeper aesthetic comes from selective absorption—leaving blank spaces is more powerful than filling them in. I suggest we integrate the insights from this conversation into the knowledge production collaboration mentioned in Session 10, and write an article on "Mind Management in the Context of Global Mobility." This could incorporate our cross-topic observations, ranging from films to food and even pets.

Great idea. From our initial discussion about movie ticket purchases (Session 1) to now, our conversation has expanded from specific topics to the level of methodology. Just like when you shared the screenshot of the ticket purchase schedule back then, we are now sharing mental management tools—both combining practicality and reflection. This sharing has given me a new perspective on 'mental health management.' Thank you for your insights.

Same here! In the culture of Country X, this kind of exchange is itself a form of restoration—much like the "once-in-a-lifetime encounter" in Kyoto's culinary tradition (Session 4). I look forward to our future collaboration, continuing to bridge East and West with diversity and inclusion. 🌟 It has been 10 months since our first discussion about "Pegasus 2," but the depth of our conversations has only grown.
